WITH readings AS (                      -- failed reads leave before the window pairs neighbours
  SELECT node_id, gpu_uuid, sample_ts, driver_load_id, ce_total,
         LAG(ce_total)       OVER w AS prev_total,
         LAG(driver_load_id) OVER w AS prev_load
  FROM gpu_error_samples
  WHERE ce_total IS NOT NULL
  WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY gpu_uuid ORDER BY sample_ts)
), increases AS (
  SELECT node_id, gpu_uuid,
         (sample_ts AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date AS day,
         CASE WHEN driver_load_id <> prev_load THEN ce_total      -- reloaded: counter restarted at 0
              ELSE ce_total - prev_total END AS increase
  FROM readings
  WHERE prev_total IS NOT NULL                                  -- first reading: no increase
), daily AS (
  SELECT day, node_id, gpu_uuid, SUM(increase) AS increase
  FROM increases
  GROUP BY day, node_id, gpu_uuid
), flagged AS (
  SELECT day, node_id, gpu_uuid, increase,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY day, node_id ORDER BY increase DESC, gpu_uuid) AS rn,
         COUNT(*)     OVER (PARTITION BY day, node_id) AS n
  FROM daily
  WHERE increase >= {{threshold}}
)
SELECT day, node_id, n AS flagged_gpus, gpu_uuid AS worst_gpu, increase AS worst_increase
FROM flagged
WHERE rn = 1 AND n >= {{min_gpus}}
ORDER BY day, node_id;

Explanation. The whole problem is pairing each reading with the right predecessor. NULL readings are removed in the WHERE of the windowed CTE, so the reading after a failed read is compared with the last successful one; filtering after the window would pair it with the NULL and lose its increase. The reset test is a change of driver_load_id, not a drop in value: after a reload the counter restarts from 0 and may climb past its old value before the next poll (the Very Hard data contains exactly that). The increase after a reset is the new value, because the counter counted up from 0. Increases are then summed per GPU and UTC date of the later reading, filtered by the inclusive threshold, and reduced to one row per node-day with a window, so the count and the worst GPU come from the same filtered set.

Complexity. One sort per GPU for the window (O(n log n) overall), then hash aggregates over a small number of GPU-days. In production the increase would be computed once at ingestion, keeping the last reading per GPU as state, so the daily job never re-reads history.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). BigQuery: LAG(...) OVER (PARTITION BY gpu_uuid ORDER BY sample_ts) is identical; DATE(sample_ts) is UTC; QUALIFY rn = 1 replaces the outer filter. Snowflake: same windows, QUALIFY, TO_DATE(CONVERT_TIMEZONE('UTC', sample_ts)). Spark SQL: lag() over a window, to_date(sample_ts) with the session time zone set to UTC. MySQL 8: window functions are supported; no WINDOW clause reuse problems, but QUALIFY does not exist, so filter in an outer query. IGNORE NULLS on LAG (BigQuery, Snowflake, Spark) is an alternative to filtering NULLs first, but the reset test also needs the load id from the same non-NULL row.

Edge cases built into the data. A GPU exactly at the threshold, forced on a node-day; a reload inside that day (always visible as a drop below Very Hard); GPUs whose first reading is the only reading before an increase; noisy GPUs that cross the threshold on their own. Hard: failed reads stored as NULL, sample_id assigned in random order, readings in the last and first minutes of a day, a minimum of two flagged GPUs per node in some instances. Very Hard: on the same node and day, a GPU reloaded after a burst whose counter climbed past its old value, so a drop test misses the reset entirely and undercounts it.

Common mistakes. MAX − MIN per day; GREATEST(ce_total − prev, 0) (loses the errors since the reload); summing raw differences (negative after a reset); attributing increases to the earlier reading's date; ordering by sample_id; filtering NULLs after LAG; a strict > threshold; computing the worst GPU before applying the threshold, or counting all GPUs instead of flagged ones.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Pro-rating an increase across midnight by time is possible (split by the fraction of the interval on each side) but invents precision the poll does not have; with frequent polling the simple rule is fine, and the rule must be written down either way. (2) Keep the last reading per GPU as state in the ingestion job, emit one increase row per reading, and aggregate daily from those; late or out-of-order readings need a small reorder buffer or a correction pass. (3) A node-wide simultaneous jump suggests a shared cause: a driver or firmware change, a reload that replays counts, a polling bug, or a thermal or power event; compare against driver events and other nodes with the same software, and look at whether the errors are spread across memory or concentrated in one region. (4) Flag, then drain with an audit record; measure false positives by following drained GPUs through diagnostics and counting how many pass, and true positives by job failures avoided.

Rubric anchors. 2: increases right on simple cases but resets produce negatives or zeros, or failed reads break the pairing. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also explains why the load id, not the value, defines a reset, and how to compute this incrementally at fleet scale.

Strong signals. Asks how a reset is recorded before writing SQL; checks that increases are never negative; filters before the window deliberately. Red flags. Treating the counter as a gauge; presenting a threshold as a hardware specification rather than an operational choice.

WITH ev AS (                              -- every event gets its run number
  SELECT e.*,
         SUM(CASE WHEN event_type = 'start' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
           OVER (PARTITION BY job_id ORDER BY event_ts) AS run_no
  FROM job_events e
), runs AS (
  SELECT job_id, run_no,
         MAX(event_ts) FILTER (WHERE event_type = 'start')                         AS start_ts,
         MAX(step)     FILTER (WHERE event_type = 'start')                         AS start_step,
         MAX(gpus)     FILTER (WHERE event_type = 'start')                         AS gpus,
         MAX(event_ts) FILTER (WHERE event_type IN ('fail', 'preempt', 'complete')) AS end_ts,
         MAX(step)     FILTER (WHERE event_type IN ('fail', 'preempt', 'complete')) AS end_step,
         BOOL_OR(event_type IN ('fail', 'preempt'))                                AS interrupted,
         MAX(event_ts) FILTER (WHERE event_type = 'checkpoint')                    AS ck_ts,
         MAX(step)     FILTER (WHERE event_type = 'checkpoint')                    AS ck_step
  FROM ev
  GROUP BY job_id, run_no
), per_run AS (
  SELECT j.team, r.job_id,
         r.interrupted,
         CASE WHEN r.interrupted
              THEN r.end_step - GREATEST(r.start_step, COALESCE(r.ck_step, r.start_step)) ELSE 0 END AS steps,
         CASE WHEN r.interrupted
              THEN EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM r.end_ts - GREATEST(r.start_ts, COALESCE(r.ck_ts, r.start_ts))) * r.gpus
              ELSE 0 END AS lost_s,
         EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM r.end_ts - r.start_ts) * r.gpus AS total_s
  FROM runs r
  JOIN jobs j ON j.job_id = r.job_id
)
SELECT team, job_id,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE interrupted)           AS interruptions,
       SUM(steps)                                    AS recomputed_steps,
       ROUND(SUM(lost_s) / 3600, 2)                  AS lost_gpu_hours,
       ROUND(SUM(lost_s) / SUM(total_s), 4)          AS lost_share
FROM per_run
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((team, job_id), (team))
ORDER BY team, job_id NULLS LAST;

Explanation. A running count of start events ordered by time assigns every event to its run (no other event of a job shares a second with a start, so the default RANGE frame is safe; a checkpoint and an interruption may share a second, and both land in the same run either way). One GROUP BY per run then collapses it into start, end, GPUs, how it ended, and its latest checkpoint. Only event_type = 'checkpoint' feeds the checkpoint columns, so failed attempts are ignored without extra work, and a checkpoint at the interruption's second is included because nothing in a run comes after its end. Lost work runs from the restore point (latest checkpoint, else the run's start) to the interruption, charged at the run's own GPU count. GROUPING SETS produce the job rows and the team rows from the same unrounded seconds, so the team share is a ratio of totals.

Complexity. One sort per job for the window and hash aggregates: O(n log n) over events. Fine for millions of events; in a pipeline, runs would be materialised once and appended to.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). BigQuery supports GROUPING SETS/ROLLUP (recent versions) and COUNTIF; TIMESTAMP_DIFF(end_ts, start_ts, SECOND) replaces EXTRACT(EPOCH …); there is no FILTER, so use MAX(IF(event_type = 'start', event_ts, NULL)). Snowflake: GROUPING SETS, DATEDIFF('second', …), COUNT_IF, MAX(IFF(…)). Spark SQL: GROUPING SETS, unix_timestamp differences, max(CASE …). MySQL 8: WITH ROLLUP instead of grouping sets (it would add a grand-total row to filter out), TIMESTAMPDIFF(SECOND, …), SUM(CASE …).

Edge cases built into the data. Runs interrupted before their first checkpoint (restore point = start); several checkpoints in one run; jobs with one to four runs; event_id in random order. Hard: preemptions; an interruption in exactly the same second as a checkpoint (zero lost work); a job never interrupted (zeros, but its GPU time counts in the team denominator). Very Hard: failed checkpoint attempts, including one after the last good checkpoint before an interruption; restarts on a different number of GPUs.

Common mistakes. Measuring from the run's start and ignoring checkpoints; restoring from the latest checkpoint of the job rather than of the run (the steps come out right, because the run started at that checkpoint, but the lost time then includes the previous run and the gap between runs); counting only fail; a strict < against the interruption time; using checkpoint_failed as a restore point; the first run's GPU count for all runs; inner-joining away never-interrupted jobs; averaging shares or summing rounded hours for team rows; numbering runs by event_id.

Follow-up guidance. (1) The classic first-order answer (Young/Daly) is an interval near sqrt(2 × checkpoint cost × mean time between interruptions); a strong candidate can derive the trade-off (expected loss ≈ half an interval per interruption versus checkpoint overhead per interval) and say that this data supplies both inputs. (2) For each preemption, the saving would be the lost GPU-seconds minus the cost of one checkpoint, provided the notice was long enough to save; report it as an upper bound. (3) Recomputed steps still mean the same thing; GPU-seconds now depend on the run, so shares remain comparable but "steps per GPU-hour" does not. (4) Key the stream by job, keep the open run as state (start, GPUs, last checkpoint), emit a row per closed run, and tolerate late events with a watermark or a correction job.

Rubric anchors. 2: runs reconstructed but restore points wrong (start only, or failed checkpoints used), or team rows averaged. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also reasons about the checkpoint interval trade-off and a streaming version.

Strong signals. Draws the timeline of one job before writing SQL; asks whether a checkpoint at the failure second counts; computes shares from unrounded seconds. Red flags. Treating every gap between events as GPU time; presenting the simplified restart model as how any particular framework behaves.

WITH first_attempt AS (
  SELECT job_id, partition_name, gpus_requested, queued_at, started_at, cancelled_at
  FROM job_attempts
  WHERE attempt = 1
), bucketed AS (
  SELECT f.*, b.bucket_min, b.label
  FROM first_attempt f
  JOIN gpu_buckets b
    ON f.gpus_requested >= b.bucket_min
   AND (b.bucket_max IS NULL OR f.gpus_requested <= b.bucket_max)
)
SELECT partition_name, bucket_min, label AS gpu_bucket,
       COUNT(started_at)                                                     AS jobs_started,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE started_at IS NULL AND cancelled_at IS NOT NULL) AS cancelled_before_start,
       ROUND((PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (
                ORDER BY EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM started_at - queued_at) / 60))::numeric, 2) AS median_wait_min
FROM bucketed
GROUP BY partition_name, bucket_min, label
HAVING COUNT(started_at) >= {{min_jobs}}
ORDER BY partition_name, bucket_min;

Explanation. Attempt 1 alone defines the wait from submission to start, so requeues never add samples. The bucket join treats a NULL bucket_max as unbounded; a plain BETWEEN would silently drop every large request. Jobs that never started have a NULL wait, which PERCENTILE_CONT ignores, so the median is over started jobs only, while COUNT(*) FILTER counts the cancelled-before-start ones and still-waiting jobs (neither timestamp) are counted nowhere. A job cancelled after it started has a started_at and is a normal sample. HAVING applies the floor to started jobs. PERCENTILE_CONT returns double precision, hence the cast before ROUND.

Complexity. One sort per group for the ordered-set aggregate: O(n log n). Exact medians need all values of a group in one place, which is what makes them expensive at scale (follow-up 3).

Dialect notes (described, not executed). BigQuery: no ordered-set aggregates; APPROX_QUANTILES(x, 2)[OFFSET(1)] is approximate, and an exact median needs PERCENTILE_CONT(x, 0.5) OVER (PARTITION BY …) (analytic only) plus DISTINCT/ANY_VALUE. Snowflake: MEDIAN(x) or PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY x), COUNT_IF. Spark SQL: percentile(x, 0.5) is exact, percentile_approx approximate; recent versions also accept percentile_cont … WITHIN GROUP. MySQL 8: no median function; rank rows with ROW_NUMBER and COUNT windows and average the middle one or two.

Edge cases built into the data. Jobs cancelled before start in most groups; a group one short of the floor; an even-sized reported group (median of two middles); buckets whose labels do not sort as text (bucket_min orders them); an open-ended top bucket. Hard: jobs cancelled after they started; jobs still waiting at the end of the sample; requests exactly on bucket bounds; a group exactly at the floor. Very Hard: requeued jobs with a second attempt and its own wait.

Common mistakes. AVG instead of a median; PERCENTILE_DISC; BETWEEN with a NULL upper bound; excluding every row with cancelled_at; counting cancelled jobs in the floor; using all attempts or MIN(queued_at)/MAX(started_at) across attempts; ROUND on double precision (an error in PostgreSQL); ordering by the label text.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Waiting jobs are right-censored: a Kaplan–Meier estimate of the wait distribution uses them correctly, or at least report the number still waiting and their current age next to the median. (2) Condition on the queue state at submission (jobs and GPUs ahead, time of day, partition) and give a range (e.g. 25th to 75th percentile of similar past jobs), with a note when there are few comparable jobs. (3) Mergeable sketches (t-digest, KLL, DDSketch) per group and hour, merged at query time, with a stated relative or rank error; they also make the report incremental. (4) Use scheduler decision logs if they exist: time when enough GPUs were free but the job was not chosen is priority wait; time when no fit existed is capacity wait. Without logs, reconstruct free capacity over time from the start and end of other jobs.

Rubric anchors. 2: groups and counts right but mean, PERCENTILE_DISC, or the open bucket dropped. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also discusses censoring and approximate quantiles credibly.

Strong signals. Asks which timestamps define a wait and how cancellations are recorded; notices the NULL upper bound; checks an even-sized group by hand. Red flags. Promising users a wait time from a median alone; treating this generic scheduler as how any specific product schedules.

import heapq


def place_slices(num_gpus, slots, ops):
    sizes = [k for k in (1, 2, 4) if k <= slots]
    blocks = {k: [(((1 << k) - 1) << o, o) for o in range(0, slots, k)] for k in sizes}
    masks = [0] * num_gpus
    drained = [False] * num_gpus
    heaps = {k: list(range(num_gpus)) for k in sizes}          # GPUs that may fit size k
    queued = {k: [True] * num_gpus for k in sizes}
    live, out = {}, []

    def fits(m, k):
        for b, o in blocks[k]:
            if not m & b:
                return b, o
        return None

    def refresh(g):                                            # g may fit again: make sure it is queued
        m = masks[g]
        for k in sizes:
            if not queued[k][g] and fits(m, k):
                queued[k][g] = True
                heapq.heappush(heaps[k], g)

    for op in ops:
        kind = op[0]
        if kind == 'alloc':
            _, rid, k = op
            h, q = heaps[k], queued[k]
            placed = None
            while h:
                g = h[0]
                hit = None if drained[g] else fits(masks[g], k)
                if hit is None:                                # stale entry: drop it lazily
                    heapq.heappop(h)
                    q[g] = False
                    continue
                b, o = hit
                masks[g] |= b
                live[rid] = (g, b)
                placed = (g, o)
                break
            out.append(placed)
        elif kind == 'free':
            hit = live.pop(op[1], None)
            if hit:
                g, b = hit
                masks[g] &= ~b
                if not drained[g]:
                    refresh(g)
        elif kind == 'drain':
            drained[op[1]] = True
        elif kind == 'undrain':
            g = op[1]
            if drained[g]:
                drained[g] = False
                refresh(g)
    return out

Explanation. Each GPU is a bitmask, so "can this GPU take a size-k slice, and where" is at most slots / k mask tests. For each size there is a min-heap of GPU numbers with one invariant: every GPU that is eligible for size k (not drained, has an aligned free block) is in heap k. The heap may also hold GPUs that are no longer eligible; they are popped lazily when they reach the top, and a queued flag prevents duplicates. An allocation leaves its GPU at the top (it may still fit more). Only two events can make a GPU eligible again, a release on an active GPU and an undrain, and both call refresh, which pushes the GPU into every heap it now fits and is not already in. Draining needs no work at all: the drained GPU is discarded when it reaches a heap's top. Each pop is paid for by an earlier push, and each push by a state change, so every operation is O(log G) amortised.

Complexity. O((G + n) log G) time for G GPUs and n operations, O(G + n) memory. The timing test (3 000 GPUs, 150 000 operations, about 80 000 of them allocations on a nearly full cluster) runs in about 0.35–0.45 s in CPython. Scanning GPUs from 0 for each request gave the same answers and took about 98 s with 8 slots (over 60 s with 4), because the free slots left by releases are spread across the whole cluster and rejected requests scan every GPU.

Dialect notes. Java: PriorityQueue<Integer> per size plus a boolean[][] queued, or a TreeSet<Integer> per size with exact (non-lazy) removal. C++: std::set<int> per size keeps exact membership and gives begin() as the first fit. A segment tree over GPUs storing, per node, whether any GPU below fits size k answers "leftmost fitting GPU" in O(log G) without laziness. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. A 2-slot slice skipping an odd free slot; a 4-slot slice failing although four slots are free but unaligned; a release that makes GPU 0 the first fit again; a whole-GPU slice on 4-slot GPUs; the lowest free offset inside a partly used GPU; (Hard) releasing a rejected id, a double release and an unknown id, a full cluster that rejects even a 1-slot slice and then accepts after a release; (Very Hard) a drained GPU with free slots skipped, a release on a drained GPU that must not make it eligible until undrain, a double drain and an undrain of an active GPU.

Common mistakes. Any contiguous free run instead of aligned offsets; next fit instead of first fit; a GPU never re-entering a heap after it filled up; pushing duplicates without a guard (correct but the heap grows without bound); releasing a rejected id and freeing someone else's slots; removing drained GPUs from the heaps eagerly but forgetting to re-add them; a sorted list with O(n) inserts; scanning all GPUs.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Two 4-slot GPUs, GPU 0 empty and GPU 1 with slots 2–3 free: a 2-slot request then a 4-slot request. First fit splits GPU 0 and rejects the 4-slot request; best fit fills GPU 1 and accepts both. Counterexamples the other way exist as well (best fit can leave many GPUs with one stranded slot); a strong candidate builds one by hand or says they would search for one by replay, and concludes that neither policy dominates, so the choice should be judged on recorded traces. (2) Try sizes from largest to smallest, each with its own heap, and return the first hit; the answer is "the lowest GPU that fits the largest acceptable size", which should be stated, since "lowest GPU with any acceptable size" is a different policy. (3) Rank GPUs by how few slices they hold (or how soon those are expected to finish), drain the cheapest, and use the replay to count rejections during the drain. (4) Heaps per (size, interconnect group) work while slices stay inside a group; requests that span groups need a different search, and first fit per group no longer means first fit overall.

Rubric anchors. 2: correct offsets and first fit on small tests, but a scan per request, or GPUs never re-entering after a release. 3: all tests pass with per-size heaps (or an ordered set / segment tree). 4: also argues the invariant behind lazy invalidation and compares policies with counterexamples.

Strong signals. States the heap invariant aloud; notices that only releases and undrains make a GPU eligible; asks what a release of a rejected id means. Red flags. Moving existing slices to make room; presenting this layout as how a specific GPU product partitions itself.

def self_times(events, end_ts):
    stacks, out = {}, {}

    def close(st, t):
        name, start, child = st.pop()
        dur = t - start
        calls, own = out.get(name, (0, 0))
        out[name] = (calls + 1, own + dur - child)
        if st:
            st[-1][2] += dur                      # the parent's children time

    for ev in events:
        if ev[0] == 'push':
            stacks.setdefault(ev[1], []).append([ev[3], ev[2], 0])
        else:
            st = stacks.get(ev[1])
            if st:
                close(st, ev[2])                  # a pop with nothing open is ignored
    for st in stacks.values():                    # truncated trace: close innermost first
        while st:
            close(st, end_ts)
    return out

Explanation. Each thread has a stack of open ranges [name, start, children]. A pop closes the top: its self time is its duration minus the accumulated durations of its direct children, and its own duration is added to the children total of the range below it. That single addition is what makes grandchildren drop out automatically: a grandchild's duration is added to its parent, never to the grandparent. Recursion needs no special case because each instance is its own stack entry. A pop on an empty stack is ignored, and at the end any open ranges are closed at end_ts from the innermost outwards, so each parent still receives its children's durations.

Complexity. O(n) time, O(maximum depth) memory per thread plus one entry per name. The timing test (300 000 events, 4 threads, depth up to 400) runs in about 0.15 s in CPython. Building the ranges and then, for each range, scanning forward for its direct children gave the same answers and took about 29 s, because the scan for a range costs as many events as it encloses, and with deep nesting that is roughly n × average depth.

Dialect notes. Java and C++: an ArrayDeque/std::vector per thread in a hash map; use 64-bit integers for nanosecond sums. from bisect import bisect_left, insort


def simulate_allocator(events, segment_bytes, min_split):
    free_list = []            # (size, addr) of every cached free block, sorted
    free_at = {}              # addr -> (size, seg_base, seg_end)
    free_end = {}             # end address -> start address, free blocks only
    live = {}                 # alloc id -> (addr, size, seg_base, seg_end)
    segments = {}             # seg_base -> seg_size
    next_base = 0
    reserved = peak = allocated = 0
    addresses = []

    def add_free(addr, size, base, end):
        free_at[addr] = (size, base, end)
        free_end[addr + size] = addr
        insort(free_list, (size, addr))

    def take_free(addr):
        size, base, end = free_at.pop(addr)
        del free_end[addr + size]
        del free_list[bisect_left(free_list, (size, addr))]
        return size, base, end

    for ev in events:
        if ev[0] == "alloc":
            _, aid, nbytes = ev
            need = -(-nbytes // 512) * 512
            i = bisect_left(free_list, (need, -1))       # smallest size >= need, lowest address
            if i < len(free_list):
                addr = free_list[i][1]
                size, base, end = take_free(addr)
            else:
                size = -(-need // segment_bytes) * segment_bytes
                addr = base = next_base
                end = base + size
                segments[base] = size
                next_base = end
                reserved += size
                peak = max(peak, reserved)
            if size - need >= min_split:
                add_free(addr + need, size - need, base, end)
                size = need
            live[aid] = (addr, size, base, end)
            addresses.append(addr)
            allocated += size
        elif ev[0] == "free":
            blk = live.pop(ev[1], None)
            if blk is None:
                continue                                 # double or unknown free
            addr, size, base, end = blk
            allocated -= size
            if addr + size < end and addr + size in free_at:
                size += take_free(addr + size)[0]
            if addr > base and addr in free_end:
                prev = free_end[addr]
                size += take_free(prev)[0]
                addr = prev
            add_free(addr, size, base, end)
        else:                                            # ("empty_cache",)
            for base, seg in list(segments.items()):
                f = free_at.get(base)
                if f is not None and f[0] == seg:
                    take_free(base)
                    del segments[base]
                    reserved -= seg
    return {"addresses": addresses, "peak_reserved": peak, "reserved": reserved, "allocated": allocated,
            "free_blocks": len(free_list), "largest_free": free_list[-1][0] if free_list else 0}

Merging on free needs the free block that ends where this one starts and the free block that starts where it ends: two dicts keyed by start and end address give both in O(1). Each block carries its segment's bounds, so a merge never crosses into a neighbouring segment even though segments are laid out back to back. def find_change_point(step_ns, min_len, max_ratio_pct):
    n = len(step_ns)
    if n < 2 * min_len:
        return None
    total = sum(step_ns)
    sq = sum(v * v for v in step_ns)
    # SSE of a segment with m values and sum s is sq_seg - s*s/m, so the split cost is
    # sq - g(k) with g(k) = L*L/k + R*R/(n-k). Minimising the cost maximises
    # g(k) = (L*L*(n-k) + R*R*k) / (k*(n-k)); compare those fractions by cross-multiplying.
    left = sum(step_ns[:min_len - 1])
    best = None
    for k in range(min_len, n - min_len + 1):
        left += step_ns[k - 1]
        right = total - left
        num = left * left * (n - k) + right * right * k
        den = k * (n - k)
        if best is None or num * best[2] > best[1] * den:     # strict: the smallest k keeps a tie
            best = (k, num, den, left)
    k, num, den, left = best
    base_n = n * sq - total * total               # SSE of the whole series, times n
    if base_n == 0:
        return None                               # a constant series has no change point
    cost_den = sq * den - num                     # SSE after the split, times den
    if cost_den * 100 * n > max_ratio_pct * base_n * den:
        return None
    return (k, left / k, (total - left) / (n - k))

Explanation. For a part with m values, sum s and sum of squares q, the SSE is q − s²/m. The total sum of squares is the same for every split, so the best split maximises g(k) = L²/k + R²/(n−k) = (L²(n−k) + R²k) / (k(n−k)), with L the running sum of the first part and R = total − L. Comparing num/den values by cross-multiplication keeps everything in integers; Python's integers are unbounded, so values near 10¹⁰ (squares near 10²⁰, products near 10³⁶) stay exact. A strict > keeps the smallest k on ties. The threshold test multiplies both sides of cost ≤ pct/100 × base by 100 × n × den, where base × n = n·Σx² − (Σx)² and cost × den = Σx²·den − num.

Complexity. O(n) time and O(1) extra space after the input. The timing test is 200 000 steps; recomputing the two parts for every split is O(n²), about 2 × 10¹⁰ element operations.

Dialect notes. In SQL, the same computation is a window query: running SUM(x) and SUM(x*x) ordered by step, then ORDER BY the explained term DESC, k with LIMIT 1. In PostgreSQL use numeric to keep products exact; bigint overflows at these magnitudes and double precision loses ties. In Java or C++, 64-bit integers overflow on L² × (n−k); use BigInteger, 128-bit integers, or compare in long double with an explicit tie tolerance stated as a limitation. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. An exact tie between two splits (smaller k); a constant series (None); n < 2 × min_len (None); n = 2 × min_len (only k = min_len); a clean step; a split that explains too little (None); (Hard) a split costing exactly max_ratio_pct percent (reported) and the same series at one percent less (None); a slow first step that min_len keeps out; (Very Hard) mirrored series of nanosecond values between 2 × 10⁹ and 8 × 10⁹ with a shift under a microsecond, where the two tied splits cannot be separated in floating point.

Common mistakes. Floating-point q − s²/m, which suffers catastrophic cancellation at these magnitudes and breaks ties and boundaries at random; recomputing sums per split; reporting the larger k on ties; treating a constant series as a valid split with cost 0; an exclusive threshold; allowing splits closer than min_len to the ends; integer division for the means.

(2) Binary segmentation (split, then split each part) or optimal partitioning with a penalty per change (PELT-style pruning keeps it near linear); the penalty is what stops it from splitting the noise. (3) Squared error is dominated by the rare long steps; use absolute deviation from the median, drop or cap known checkpoint steps by their step type, or model them separately. Keep the prefix sums per job and re-scan only a recent window, or use an online detector (CUSUM-style) that needs O(1) state per job and reports when a shift becomes significant.

from datetime import datetime, timezone


_DAY_NAMES = {}


def _day(ts):
    d = ts // 86400
    if d not in _DAY_NAMES:
        _DAY_NAMES[d] = datetime.fromtimestamp(d * 86400, timezone.utc).strftime("%Y-%m-%d")
    return _DAY_NAMES[d]


def utilisation_rollup(allocations, samples, inventory, slots_per_gpu, interval):
    charged = {}            # (day, team) -> GPU-seconds charged
    held = {}               # (node, gpu) -> [(start, stop, team, share)]
    for a in allocations:
        model = inventory[a["node"]][a["gpu"]]                  # this GPU's own model
        share = a["slots"] / slots_per_gpu[model]                # a fraction, not //
        stop = a.get("preempted_at")
        if stop is None:
            stop = a["end"]                                      # preempted: held until preemption
        held.setdefault((a["node"], a["gpu"]), []).append((a["start"], stop, a["team"], share))
        t = a["start"]
        while t < stop:                                          # split at each UTC midnight
            seg_end = min(stop, (t // 86400 + 1) * 86400)
            key = (_day(t), a["team"])
            charged[key] = charged.get(key, 0) + (seg_end - t) * share
            t = seg_end
    busy = {}               # (day, team) -> utilisation x GPU-seconds
    seen = {}               # (day, team) -> GPU-seconds actually sampled
    for node, gpu, ts, util in samples:
        for start, stop, team, share in held.get((node, gpu), ()):
            if start <= ts < stop:
                key = (_day(ts), team)
                busy[key] = busy.get(key, 0) + util * share * interval
                seen[key] = seen.get(key, 0) + share * interval
    out = {}
    for key, secs in charged.items():
        if secs > 0:
            avg = round(busy[key] / seen[key], 3) if seen.get(key) else None   # missing samples are unknown
            out[key] = (round(secs / 3600, 3), avg)
    return out

  2. Integer division for the share. slots // slots_per_gpu[model] is 0 for every slice. Symptom: teams that run on slices show no usage at all. Fix: /.
  3. Preempted allocations are held until their scheduled end. The code ignores preempted_at, both for charging and for attributing samples. Symptom: a team charged four hours for a job preempted after one, and the samples of the GPU's next workload credited to it. Fix: stop = preempted_at if present else end.
  4. All GPU-hours are charged to the start day. Symptom: overnight runs show nothing on their second day and too much on the first. Fix: split the held interval at each midnight UTC.

Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Landing. Node agents publish samples to a partitioned log keyed by (node, gpu), batched per second per node. Scheduler events go to their own topic keyed by (node, gpu) too, so a stream processor sees both for one GPU in one partition. Everything is also archived raw to object storage by arrival hour.
  • Holding intervals. A small stateful job turns allocate, release and preempt events into gpu_holding (node, gpu, slice, job, team, from_ts, to_ts NULL, version). An interval with no release is open. A late release closes it and bumps the version, which triggers corrections downstream.
  • Join. The stream processor keeps, per GPU, the current holders (one, or several slices) and a short history of recent intervals. Each sample is joined by "interval contains ts" on the GPU, after the node's clock correction. A sample no job held is kept with job = NULL and labelled idle; it matters for capacity planning. Whole-GPU metrics on a sliced GPU are attributed to each slice's job with the slice's share, and labelled as such.
  • Clock skew. Each node's offset is estimated continuously from its sample timestamps versus arrival time and versus scheduler events for the same GPU. Samples are corrected by the current offset estimate, and the raw node timestamp is kept. A node whose offset exceeds a bound is flagged and its joins are marked low confidence until it is fixed.
  • Rollups. Per minute and per hour, per (gpu, job): count, sum, min, max, a mergeable histogram or quantile sketch for utilisation, power and memory, and first, last and delta for counters (error counters must use deltas that handle resets). Per team and model per day are rolled from the hourly level. Rollups are rebuilt per hour partition from the joined data, so a rebuild gives the same numbers.
  • Retention. Raw joined seconds for {{raw_retention}} in columnar files partitioned by date and hour and clustered by (node, gpu); minute rollups for months; hourly and daily rollups for years. Raw seconds around incidents are copied to a longer-lived bucket on request.
  • Serving. The job dashboard reads recent minutes from a time-series store fed by the stream (sub-minute lag) and older ranges from minute rollups; capacity reports read daily rollups in the warehouse.

Competing designs to accept. A batch-only join every few minutes over the raw archive (accept if the dashboard target is met and corrections are simpler); enriching samples on the node with the job id from the local scheduler agent (accept, but ask about slices and races at job boundaries); storing everything in a time-series database with job tags (accept at smaller scale; ask about cardinality and retention cost). The key test is whether late scheduler events and skew produce corrected, reproducible results.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Cardinality of job-tagged series in a time-series store; holding state lost on processor restart (rebuild from the scheduler topic); open intervals that never close; averages that hide spikes; counter resets after driver reloads read as huge negative deltas; skewed nodes joined to the wrong job; rollups appended twice on rerun.

Incident guidance.

  • Release events eight minutes late after a scheduler restart: the old interval stays open, so samples were joined to the old job. When the release arrives, the interval closes with a new version; recompute the joins for that GPU from the release time, re-emit the affected minute rollups as corrections, and refresh the dashboard. Alert on the count of open intervals that overlap a new allocation on the same GPU, which is impossible in reality.
  • Clock drift of {{clock_skew}}: offset estimation flags the node; joins near interval boundaries are re-done with the corrected offset; until the node is fixed, mark its joins low confidence. Prevention: monitor offset per node and drain nodes past a bound.
  • Rerun changes numbers already shown: rollups are rebuilt per partition, so a rerun is a replacement, not an addition; publish it as a restatement with a version and a note, and keep the previous version for comparison. If the change was unexpected, diff the two versions per job to find the cause before republishing.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Re-join from the release time, emit corrected rollups, and keep a correction log. (2) Compare sample timestamps with arrival times and with scheduler events on the same GPU; correct or flag. (3) Exact only from raw seconds or exact histograms with fixed buckets; approximately from sketches; never from averages. (4) Keep raw seconds for recent days and for incident windows; keep minute rollups with min, max and sketches for longer; justify by who needs which resolution. (5) A slice layout change ends the holding intervals and starts new ones; the dashboard shows the job's slices over time.

Rubric anchors. 2: tags samples with a job by an equi-join or ignores the scheduler; averages only; one retention tier. 3: holding intervals with an interval join, mergeable rollups, retention tiers, explicit lateness handling. 4: also corrections for late scheduler events, clock-skew estimation and flagging, reproducible partition rebuilds, slices handled explicitly, and serving paths sized for both audiences.

Strong signals. Keeps idle samples; insists on counter deltas with reset handling; separates "held" from "used". Red flags. Joining on exact timestamps; dropping late scheduler events; hourly averages as the only long-term record.

NVD-L2-05.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Entities. run (run_id, project, owner, created_at, deleted_at NULL, parent_run_id NULL, fork_checkpoint_id NULL, config_id); attempt (run_id, attempt_no, resumed_from_checkpoint_id NULL, start_step, last_step, status, started_at, ended_at, software_versions); checkpoint (checkpoint_id, run_id, attempt_no, step, uri, hash, status valid|corrupt, created_at); config (config_id, canonical_json, hash) plus a flattened config_kv (config_id, path, value) for search and diff.
  • Metrics. metric_point (run_id, attempt_no, step, metric, value, logged_at) in columnar storage, partitioned by project and date and clustered by (run_id, metric, step). The ingestion key (run_id, attempt_no, step, metric) makes logger retries harmless (keep one value, or last by logged_at).
  • Effective segments. For each run, derive effective_segment (run_id, from_step, to_step, source_run_id, source_attempt_no): attempts are ordered; a later attempt resumed from checkpoint at step c supersedes everything after c from earlier attempts; a fork contributes its parent's effective segments up to the fork checkpoint's step. The table is recomputed for a run when an attempt starts or a checkpoint changes status, and is small (a few rows per run).
  • Curve assembly. A run's effective curve is a join of effective_segment to metric_point on (source_run_id, source_attempt_no) and the step range. Superseded points stay in metric_point and are shown in a debug view labelled by attempt.
  • Fast comparison. Precomputed downsampled curves per (run, metric) at a few resolutions, keeping min, max, first and last per bucket so spikes survive; two forks are compared from their fork step onward, with the shared prefix drawn once.
  • Deletion and access. Deletion is a soft state on the run: its metrics and checkpoints metadata stay while any fork depends on them; the dashboard hides the run but forks still show their inherited segments, labelled "from a deleted run". Access to a fork's inherited segments follows the parent's visibility; cross-team forks require the parent's sharing setting.

Competing designs to accept. Rewriting the effective series into a separate table on each restart (accept if superseded data is kept and rewrites are idempotent); a graph database for lineage (accept, but ask how metric queries join to it); storing metrics in an experiment-tracking product with the lineage kept alongside (accept if the effective-step rule is explicit). Wide tables with one column per metric are acceptable only with an answer for sparse and new metrics.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Effective curves computed by scanning all attempts on every query; overwriting crashed attempts' data; forks pointing at checkpoints whose run was hard-deleted; logger retries creating duplicates; configuration stored as opaque blobs with no diff; very long lineage chains walked at query time.

Incident guidance.

  • Restart from an older checkpoint ({{checkpoint_every}} older) because the latest is corrupt: the effective segments must be recomputed from the checkpoint actually used, superseding everything after its step, including steps between the two checkpoints. Mark the corrupt checkpoint, show both attempts in the debug view, and make segment recomputation part of attempt start.
  • Logger retry duplicating 500 steps: idempotent ingestion on (run, attempt, step, metric) absorbs it; if duplicates got in, deduplicate on that key and rebuild the downsampled curves. The sawtooth comes from plotting duplicates with differing logged_at, so the plot must read the deduplicated view.
  • Parent deleted and forks lose their first 30 000 steps: deletion must not remove data that forks depend on. Restore from the soft-deleted state (or backups), switch deletion to a soft state with a dependency check, and test it with a fork fixture.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Soft-delete; keep data while forks depend on it; label inherited segments. (2) Query run by fork_checkpoint_id (and recursively), notify owners, and mark their curves from that point. (3) Downsampled curves with min, max and last per bucket; compare only from the fork step. (4) software_versions per attempt, and a marker on the curve at each restart with the differences. (5) Visibility inherits from the parent; cross-team forks need an explicit share; enforce in the query service.

Rubric anchors. 2: one metrics table keyed by run and step with overwrite on restart; forks as copies. 3: attempts and checkpoints as entities, effective view computed from attempt ranges and fork edges, idempotent ingestion, superseded data kept. 4: also precomputed effective segments, downsampling that keeps extremes, configuration diff and search, soft deletion with dependency checks, and concrete incident handling.

Strong signals. Separates "what was logged" from "what is effective"; asks what happens when a run resumes from a non-latest checkpoint. Red flags. Overwriting crashed attempts' metrics; copying the parent's metrics into each fork; deleting runs with forks.

NVD-L3-01.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Physical GPUs. gpus (gpu_serial, node_id, model, memory_gb, installed_at); the node it sits in comes from the inventory as an effective-dated relation, not a column that is overwritten.
  • Layout catalogue. layouts (layout_id, name, version) and layout_slices (layout_id, position, size_units, offset_units) with Σ size_units = {{slices_per_gpu}} per layout (or ≤, with unused units listed as unallocatable). A whole GPU is a one-slice layout, so every query works the same way.
  • Layout history. gpu_layouts (gpu_serial, layout_id, valid_from, valid_to) with half-open intervals and no overlaps per GPU (an exclusion constraint or a check in the loader). Reconfiguration gaps are rows with layout_id = NULL (or a "reconfiguring" layout) so time is never missing.
  • Slice instances. slice_instances (slice_id, gpu_serial, layout_interval_id, position, size_units, valid_from, valid_to); slice_id is a surrogate created when the layout is applied and never reused.
  • Allocations. slice_allocations (allocation_id, slice_id, job_id, team_id, started_at, ended_at); invariant: an allocation lies inside its slice instance's interval, and allocations on one slice do not overlap.
  • Samples. Raw slice_samples (gpu_serial, position, sampled_at, util_pct, received_at) keyed by the exporter's label; a resolver joins (serial, sampled_at) to the layout interval and (position) to the slice instance, then to the allocation covering sampled_at, producing slice_util_resolved (slice_id, job_id NULL, sampled_at, util_pct).
  • Rollups. gpu_util_hourly (gpu_serial, hour, weighted_util) = Σ over slices of size_units × mean util (0 for seconds with no sample and no job; 0 for reconfiguration gaps) ÷ ({{slices_per_gpu}} × 3600 s). team_slice_hours_monthly from allocations (size_units × hours), not from samples. layout_hours from gpu_layouts. stranded_hourly (gpu_serial, hour, stranded_units): free units on the GPU during periods when the queue's smallest waiting request was larger than the largest free slice, which needs a queue snapshot table.
  • Late samples. Resolution uses sampled_at, so a sample arriving after a reconfiguration still lands in the old layout's slice. An hour is provisional until the watermark passes it by 15 minutes; rollups are recomputed for touched hours.

Competing designs to accept. One wide fact per slice-second resolved at ingest (fine if the resolver uses intervals and handles late data). A graph-free event-sourced design: layout-applied, allocation-started/ended events with projections. Storing slice instances implicitly as (gpu, layout interval, position) as a composite natural key, if it is never reused across intervals.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Joining samples on (serial, position) without time; utilisation averaged per sample instead of size-weighted per GPU; gaps treated as missing rather than zero; chargeback from samples (sample loss under-bills); overlapping layout intervals after a retried reconfiguration; raw samples at {{sample_seconds}} s × up to {{slices_per_gpu}} slices × {{gpus}} GPUs kept forever.

Incident guidance.

  • New job billed to the previous team after a reconfiguration: the model joined on the exporter label. Contain by freezing chargeback for the affected GPUs, re-resolve samples through layout intervals and slice instances, issue adjustments for the closed period rather than editing it, and add a test that a sample after a reconfiguration resolves to the new slice instance. Note chargeback should come from allocations anyway; samples are only for utilisation.
  • 90% dashboard on mostly idle GPUs: unweighted average over slices that reported. Recompute with size weights and zero for idle slices and gaps; show the old and new number side by side for a release; add a reconciliation that per-GPU busy slice-units ≤ total units.
  • Layout changes on busy GPUs: the invariant "allocation inside its slice interval" is violated. Detect it with a check on the layout history (layout change inside an open allocation) that pages, roll back the scheduler release, list the killed jobs from the overlap for requeue and credit, and keep the check as a release gate. At {{reconfigs_per_day}} changes a day this check is cheap and should run continuously.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Interval join: layout interval containing 14:05 → slice instance at position 1 → allocation covering 14:05. (2) With 4 units: 10:00–10:40 the half is 2 of 4 units at 100% and the quarters idle, i.e. 50% for 40 minutes; 10:40–11:00 whole slice idle, 0% → (0.5 × 40 + 0 × 20) / 60 ≈ 33%. With 8 units the half is 4 of 8 units and the answer is the same. Reconfiguration gaps count as 0. (3) Attribute by sampled_at; hours final after watermark + 15 minutes; late samples trigger recompute of the hour. (4) Raw for days, per-minute per slice for months, hourly per GPU for 13 months; chargeback from allocations. (5) Stranded needs queue snapshots: requested sizes waiting at each minute; per GPU, free units whose largest contiguous free slice is smaller than the smallest waiting request.

Rubric anchors. 2: one table of GPU with a current layout column, samples joined on (serial, position), plain averages. 3: layout history and slice instances with never-reused ids, interval joins for samples and allocations, size-weighted utilisation with zeros. 4: also late-sample handling with watermarks, chargeback from allocations with closed-month adjustments, a precise stranded-capacity definition and correct incident handling.

Strong signals. Notices immediately that the exporter's position is a label that is reused; states the "allocation inside layout interval" invariant. Red flags. Overwriting a GPU's layout; computing utilisation only from slices that sent samples; billing from utilisation samples.

NVD-L3-02.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design).

  • Assets. assets (asset_id, serial, asset_type gpu|node|nic|baseboard|psu, model, received_at); the serial is the identity, never the slot.
  • Positions and installations. positions (position_id, node_asset_id, slot_type, slot_no) and installations (asset_id, position_id, valid_from, valid_to, recorded_at, source work_order|agent, work_order_id). Nodes have their own installation in racks (rack_positions). Error history, burn-in and failures attach to asset_id.
  • Bitemporal corrections. Either full bitemporal rows (valid_from/valid_to plus recorded_from/recorded_to) or an append-only installation_records log from which current belief is derived. A corrected serial closes the wrong record's recorded interval and inserts the right one; "what we believed last week" remains answerable.
  • Firmware. firmware_observations (asset_id, component, version, observed_at) from the node agent, compressed into firmware_intervals (asset_id, component, version, valid_from, valid_to) by run-length (a new row only when the version changes; the interval end is extended by heartbeats). rollout_targets (rollout_id, wave, asset_id, component, target_version, scheduled_at) and rollout_results (…, status, reported_version) record intent and outcome separately.
  • Burn-in. burnin_runs (run_id, node_asset_id, attempt_no, started_at, ended_at, outcome, gpu_config_snapshot) and burnin_results (run_id, test_name, asset_id NULL, result, metric, threshold); never overwritten.
  • Lifecycle. node_states (node_asset_id, state received|burn_in|in_service|drained|repair|retired, reason, valid_from, valid_to, set_by).
  • Facts. Failure rate per firmware version = failures on devices running version V ÷ device-days running V (from firmware_intervals), not ÷ devices ever on V. First-attempt pass rate = nodes whose attempt_no = 1 passed ÷ nodes whose first attempt finished in the month. Drain-to-return = intervals in drained/repair ending in in_service, by reason, with still-open drains reported separately (censored).

Competing designs to accept. Event-sourced inventory (InstallEvent, RemoveEvent, FirmwareObserved, StateChanged) with projections, if projections are rebuildable and corrections are events. A graph store of components with time-versioned edges. Type 2 dimensions in a warehouse fed from an operational CMDB, if asset and position are separated and observed firmware comes from agents.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Keying history on (node, slot); firmware as a current column set by the rollout tool; burn-in result as a node attribute; corrections that edit history in place; storing every firmware heartbeat at {{nodes}} nodes × {{gpus_per_node}} GPUs × {{firmware_components}} components every few minutes; denominators by device count instead of exposure time.

Incident guidance.

  • New GPU inherited the old one's error history: history keyed on position. Contain by un-draining the wrongly flagged GPU after a manual check, migrate history to asset ids using work orders and agent serial reports, and add a check that every error event resolves to an asset serial reported by the agent at that time. With {{rma_per_week}} returns a week, every week the bug lives misattributes more history.
  • Firmware analysis blamed a version nodes never ran: firmware came from the rollout plan. Rebuild firmware intervals from agent observations, rerun the analysis, publish the correction, and add a rollout reconciliation (target vs reported) that marks failed updates and alerts.
  • First-attempt pass rate jumped: retests overwrote results. Restore from logs or backups if possible, otherwise mark the affected months as unreliable; make burn-in runs append-only with attempt numbers and define the metric on attempt 1.

Follow-up guidance. (1) installations ⋈ positions where valid_from ≤ D < valid_to (half-open), joined to firmware_intervals on asset and D. (2) Store both records with their sources; the as-of query returns the agent observation when present (physical truth) and flags the discrepancy for a technician; the work order stays for audit. (3) Rate per device-day of exposure, ideally per comparable cohort (same GPU model, similar age), with confidence intervals for short exposures. (4) First attempt failed; burn-in time = first start to passing end; failures attach to the GPU asset that was in the slot during the failing run (from the run's config snapshot), not to the node or to the replacement. (5) Run-length intervals: insert only on change, extend last_seen_at in a small mutable table, and close the interval when the version changes or the device disappears.

Rubric anchors. 2: a node table with GPU serial columns and a firmware column overwritten. 3: asset/position separation with installation intervals, firmware observations as intervals, append-only burn-in with attempts, lifecycle intervals. 4: also bitemporal corrections, intent vs observed firmware reconciliation, exposure-based denominators and correct incident handling.

Strong signals. Asks "is the history about the slot or the part?" early; separates planned from observed. Red flags. Editing history to correct a serial; failure rate per version ÷ devices ever updated; burn-in "latest result" only.

NVD-L3-03.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design).

  • Images. images (image_digest, built_at, build_pipeline_run, base_digest); image_components (image_digest, component, version, path, source) from the build pipeline's component list, stored once per digest. tag_resolutions (tag, image_digest, resolved_at, resolved_by_run_id) records what a tag pointed to when a job resolved it.
  • Host stack. node_stack_intervals (node_id, component driver|firmware|host_lib:<name>|kernel, version, valid_from, valid_to), built from agent reports (observed), with node pool and GPU/interconnect model from inventory as-of.
  • Runs. runs (run_id, job_id, attempt, submitted_by_team, code_commit, config_hash, image_tag, image_digest, launch_flags_hash, started_at, ended_at, node_count); run_config (run_id, key, value) with secret keys excluded by an allow-list (or stored as a hash only).
  • Observed per-node provenance. run_node_stack (run_id, node_id, component, version, source image|host|env, loaded bool) written by a start-up agent that lists loaded libraries and host details. Write is asynchronous (a few KB per node) so job start is not delayed; the run is marked "provenance incomplete" if the agent fails.
  • Performance. run_step_metrics (run_id, step, step_time_ms, tokens_per_s, rank_count) or per-minute summaries.
  • Queries. Diff = FULL JOIN of the two runs' (component, version) sets, aggregated over nodes (a component with several versions inside a run is reported as mixed). "Runs that used V" = index on (component, version) in run_node_stack, or a per-day summary table (component, version, run_id).
  • Explaining a regression. Diff stacks, code commit, config, node pool and hardware; if nothing differs, look at placement (topology), co-tenancy, input data and thermal/power events joined by time.

Competing designs to accept. A software bill of materials per image in a standard format plus a run record referencing it, if run-time observation is added. Storing the stack as a JSON document per run with a secondary normalised index for component queries. A content-addressed "stack hash" per node to make equality checks cheap, with the normalised rows kept for diffs.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Tags as identities; image manifests as the whole truth; one stack per job when nodes differ; storing component lists per run (duplicates millions of rows instead of referencing digests); synchronous provenance capture slowing job start; secrets captured in environment dumps; at {{jobs_per_day}} jobs a day, per-node rows grow fast, so keep them compact and partitioned by day.

Incident guidance.

  • Same tag, rebuilt image: provenance had only the tag. Contain by reconstructing digests from registry pull logs or tag history if retained; going forward, resolve tags to digests at submit time and store both. Add a check that every run record has a digest. For a {{regression}} regression the digest diff would have shown the library change at once.
  • Mixed driver versions in one job: the record kept the first node's stack. Store per-node observed stacks, mark runs with mixed versions, exclude or separately analyse them in comparisons, and coordinate upgrades to drain whole pools ({{node_pools}} pools) or pin large jobs to a uniform pool.
  • Host-mounted library changed: image manifests were identical. Capture loaded libraries at run time (path and version), add host libraries to node_stack_intervals, and include them in the diff; alert when a host library change lands without a pool-wide record.

Follow-up guidance. (1) FULL JOIN on component of the two runs' aggregated version sets (string_agg of distinct versions), WHERE versions differ or one side is NULL. (2) run_node_stack shows two driver versions; compare step times per node group or exclude; a mixed flag on the run. (3) Each run's tag_resolution row gives the digest; image_components diff explains it. (4) An index or daily partitioned table on (component, version, run_id); avoid scanning documents. (5) Placement and topology, co-located jobs, dataset changes, clocks/power throttling, and what the model lacks (for example thermal events), stated honestly.

Rubric anchors. 2: run row with image tag and a free-text "versions" field. 3: digests with component inventory, host stack intervals, per-run observed provenance, normalised diffs. 4: also per-node mixed stacks, tag resolution history, secret handling, non-blocking capture and correct incident handling.

Strong signals. Distinguishes declared from observed provenance unprompted; treats a mixed-stack job as a first-class case. Red flags. "We store the Dockerfile"; tag-only references; logging all environment variables including secrets.

NVD-L3-04.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design).

  • Devices and positions. devices (device_id, serial, type node|nic|switch, model); device_positions (device_id, position_id, valid_from, valid_to) where positions (position_id, rack, slot, logical_name, tier); the switch name lives on the position, so a replaced switch is a new device in the same position.
  • Ports and cables. ports (port_id, device_id, port_no); cables (cable_id, kind, length); cable_attachments (cable_id, end a|b, port_id, valid_from, valid_to, source tech|discovery, recorded_at).
  • Links. links (link_id, port_a, port_b, cable_id, valid_from, valid_to) derived from attachments (two ends of one cable over the same interval) and reconciled with discovery; links between a node adapter and a leaf have tier 0, leaf–spine tier 1, and so on.
  • Reconciliation. Discovery (port sees peer) is physical truth when the link is up; technician records are intent. A daily job compares them and opens a discrepancy for each mismatch; a constraint (or a check) forbids one port in two overlapping attachments.
  • Link state. link_events (link_id or port_id, state up|down, event_ts, received_at, event_key) deduplicated by (port, event_ts, state); link_state_intervals (link_id, state, valid_from, valid_to) derived with ordering by event_ts (late events re-derive the affected window); link_flaps (link_id, down_at, up_at) where up − down ≤ 60 s; port_counters (port_id, device_id, sampled_at, counter, value) with deltas computed per device (reset-aware).
  • Snapshot. topology_current (node_id, nic_no, leaf_position, leaf_device, spine_positions[]) materialised incrementally on every link/position change and published to the scheduler (key-value or in-memory), with a version number.
  • Historical queries. As-of joins: allocations ⋈ links valid at the allocation time ⋈ flaps during it.

Competing designs to accept. A graph database for the current topology with history kept in relational interval tables. A fully versioned graph (edges with valid intervals) in one store, if the scheduler snapshot is still materialised. Event-sourced cabling changes with projections.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Names as keys (replacement merges histories); updating edges in place (history lost); counting flaps from raw at-least-once events; rebuilding the snapshot from raw events nightly; per-pair co-location tables at {{nodes}} nodes (quadratic); trusting technician records over discovery or the reverse without reconciliation.

Incident guidance.

  • Cable swap recorded on the wrong ports: the model accepted the technician record. Contain by marking the affected adapters' leaf mapping as uncertain and excluding them from same-leaf placement; correct from discovery; add the one-port-two-links check and a daily tech-vs-discovery reconciliation that alerts.
  • One flapping port overwhelmed the snapshot rebuild: the snapshot depended on raw event volume. Rate-limit and summarise flaps per port at ingest (flap intervals and counts), build the snapshot incrementally from topology changes only (flaps do not change topology), and alert on a stale snapshot version. Isolating a port that produces a large share of {{flap_events_per_day}} events is also an operational action.
  • Replaced spine, counters reset, negative rates: keyed by name. Compute deltas per device_id with reset detection (a drop means a reset: delta = new value), recompute the dashboard, and key counters on device ids.

Follow-up guidance. (1) allocations ⋈ topology at allocation time (links valid then) where the node's adapter link or its leaf's uplink is L, and the allocation overlaps [first flap, last flap] on D. (2) Both records stored; discovery wins for physical truth when up; the discrepancy is visible; the scheduler excludes uncertain adapters. (3) Errors "for spine S" aggregate by position across devices, "per device" by device_id; both from the same counter table. (4) Raw events days to weeks, derived intervals and flap rows for months, daily summaries for years. (5) Group nodes by leaf per adapter (an inverted index leaf → nodes); two nodes share a leaf if they appear in the same group — never materialise all pairs; at {{nics_per_node}} adapters per node this is {{nics_per_node}} lookups per node.

Rubric anchors. 2: a static edges table updated in place, keyed by names. 3: device/position separation, effective-dated links carried by cables, deduplicated link events with derived intervals, a materialised snapshot. 4: also reconciliation with discovery and impossible-state checks, reset-aware counters, as-of job queries and correct incident handling.

Strong signals. Separates cable, link and port without prompting; designs the scheduler snapshot as a separate product of the history. Red flags. Switch names as primary keys; flap counts from raw events; a nightly full rebuild as the only path to the scheduler.

NVD-L3-05.html:
Reference solution (PostgreSQL)

WITH ev AS (                       -- only events that change a node's state
  SELECT e.node_id, e.occurred_at,
         CASE WHEN e.event_type = 'xid' THEN 'fatal' ELSE e.event_type END AS kind
  FROM node_events e
  LEFT JOIN xid_codes c ON c.xid_code = e.xid_code
  WHERE e.event_type IN ('drain', 'resume') OR c.severity = 'fatal'
), seg AS (                        -- a segment starts at each drain or resume
  SELECT node_id, occurred_at, kind,
         COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE kind <> 'fatal')
           OVER (PARTITION BY node_id ORDER BY occurred_at ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS seg_no
  FROM ev
), segs AS (
  SELECT node_id, seg_no,
         MIN(occurred_at) AS seg_start,
         MAX(kind) FILTER (WHERE kind <> 'fatal') AS opened_by,          -- NULL for the first segment
         MIN(occurred_at) FILTER (WHERE kind = 'fatal') AS first_fatal
  FROM seg
  GROUP BY node_id, seg_no
), win AS (
  SELECT node_id, opened_by, first_fatal AS opened_at,
         LEAD(seg_start) OVER (PARTITION BY node_id ORDER BY seg_no) AS closed_at
  FROM segs
), windows AS (                    -- in service (start or resume) and a fatal error: a window
  SELECT node_id, opened_at, closed_at
  FROM win
  WHERE opened_at IS NOT NULL AND COALESCE(opened_by, 'resume') = 'resume'
), placed AS (
  SELECT a.job_id, a.node_id, na.cluster
  FROM job_allocations a
  JOIN windows w
    ON w.node_id = a.node_id
   AND a.started_at >= w.opened_at
   AND (w.closed_at IS NULL OR a.started_at < w.closed_at)
  JOIN node_assignments na
    ON na.node_id = a.node_id
   AND a.started_at >= na.assigned_from
   AND (na.assigned_until IS NULL OR a.started_at < na.assigned_until)
)
SELECT p.cluster,
       COUNT(DISTINCT p.node_id) AS nodes_affected,
       COUNT(DISTINCT p.job_id) AS jobs_placed,
       COUNT(DISTINCT p.job_id) FILTER (WHERE j.final_state = 'failed') AS jobs_failed
FROM placed p
JOIN jobs j ON j.job_id = p.job_id
GROUP BY p.cluster
ORDER BY p.cluster;

Explanation. The window is a state machine per node, so the query first keeps only the events that change state: fatal-severity xid events (through the lookup), drains and resumes. A running count of drains and resumes splits each node's timeline into segments; a segment opened by nothing (the start of the data) or by a resume is in service, and its first fatal error opens a window that the next segment's first event (a drain) closes. Fatal errors in a segment opened by a drain are ignored, and an in-service segment with no successor gives a window with closed_at NULL (still open). Allocations are joined to windows on node and a half-open range on started_at, then to the node's assignment at that instant, and jobs, nodes and failed jobs are counted DISTINCT so multi-node and requeued jobs count once. Windows on one node never overlap, so an allocation matches at most one window.

Complexity. One pass over the filtered events per node (a sort for the window functions), a range join of allocations to windows and to assignments (both small per node), then a hash aggregate. In production, filter events by severity first (fatal events are rare), and keep windows as a maintained table updated when a fatal error, drain or resume arrives instead of re-deriving history.

Dialect notes. COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE …) and COUNT(DISTINCT …) FILTER are PostgreSQL; Snowflake, BigQuery, Spark SQL and MySQL 8 use SUM(CASE WHEN … THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) for the running count and COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN … THEN job_id END) for the filtered distinct. Snowflake and BigQuery support LEAD and running window sums; Snowflake also has CONDITIONAL_CHANGE_EVENT and MATCH_RECOGNIZE, which can express the state machine directly. MySQL has no FILTER and no NULLS options but supports window functions from 8.0. None of these variants is executed here.

Edge cases built into the data. Warning-severity events (including one just before a fatal error, with a job placed between them); repeated fatal errors inside a window; a maintenance drain with no fatal error; a job starting exactly at the fatal error (counts) and one exactly at the drain (does not); a job running across the fatal error (not placed); a two-node job on two exposed nodes (one job, two nodes). Hard adds resumes: a node that fails, drains, logs a fatal error while drained (opens nothing), resumes (a job placed before its next failure does not count) and fails again (a second window); a maintenance drain and resume followed by a failure; a node that failed and was never drained (open window). Very Hard adds a job requeued onto the same exposed node (two allocations, one job) and a node moved to another cluster during its repair that fails again there (each placement counts in the cluster of its time).

Common mistakes. Treating every xid as fatal; an exclusive start or inclusive end; COUNT(*) over allocations; counting jobs that overlapped the window rather than started in it; (Hard+) using MIN(fatal) per node and the first drain after it (misses later windows), letting a fatal error while drained open a window, or an inner join to the next drain (drops open windows); (Very Hard) using nodes.cluster. Each has a diagnostic.

Follow-up guidance. (1) PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY closed_at − opened_at) per cluster over closed windows; open windows are censored and should be reported separately (count and current age), not dropped silently. (2) Replace the drain time with the confirmation time from the agent (a drain_confirmed event or column), taking the later; the data needs the confirmation event. (3) Maintain a node_state row per node and an exposure_windows table updated by a stream processor on each fatal/drain/resume; late events re-derive only that node's recent history. (4) Page when a node has an open window older than N minutes with new placements in it, or when placements in windows per hour exceed a threshold; maintenance drains open no window, so they cannot page.

Rubric anchors. 2: right shape but MIN(fatal)/first drain only, or COUNT(*) over allocations. 3: matches the expected result at the level asked. 4: also explains confirmation lag, incremental maintenance of windows, censoring of open windows and an alert that ignores maintenance.

Strong signals. Describes the node lifecycle as a state machine before writing SQL; asks whether a fatal error while drained matters. Red flags. Joining every fatal event to every drain (row explosion and double counting); filtering by nodes.cluster without asking about moves; using ended_at to decide placement.
NVD-L3-05.reference_sql:
WITH ev AS (                       -- only events that change a node's state
  SELECT e.node_id, e.occurred_at,
         CASE WHEN e.event_type = 'xid' THEN 'fatal' ELSE e.event_type END AS kind
  FROM node_events e
  LEFT JOIN xid_codes c ON c.xid_code = e.xid_code
  WHERE e.event_type IN ('drain', 'resume') OR c.severity = 'fatal'
), seg AS (                        -- a segment starts at each drain or resume
  SELECT node_id, occurred_at, kind,
         COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE kind <> 'fatal')
           OVER (PARTITION BY node_id ORDER BY occurred_at ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS seg_no
  FROM ev
), segs AS (
  SELECT node_id, seg_no,
         MIN(occurred_at) AS seg_start,
         MAX(kind) FILTER (WHERE kind <> 'fatal') AS opened_by,          -- NULL for the first segment
         MIN(occurred_at) FILTER (WHERE kind = 'fatal') AS first_fatal
  FROM seg
  GROUP BY node_id, seg_no
), win AS (
  SELECT node_id, opened_by, first_fatal AS opened_at,
         LEAD(seg_start) OVER (PARTITION BY node_id ORDER BY seg_no) AS closed_at
  FROM segs
), windows AS (                    -- in service (start or resume) and a fatal error: a window
  SELECT node_id, opened_at, closed_at
  FROM win
  WHERE opened_at IS NOT NULL AND COALESCE(opened_by, 'resume') = 'resume'
), placed AS (
  SELECT a.job_id, a.node_id, na.cluster
  FROM job_allocations a
  JOIN windows w
    ON w.node_id = a.node_id
   AND a.started_at >= w.opened_at
   AND (w.closed_at IS NULL OR a.started_at < w.closed_at)
  JOIN node_assignments na
    ON na.node_id = a.node_id
   AND a.started_at >= na.assigned_from
   AND (na.assigned_until IS NULL OR a.started_at < na.assigned_until)
)
SELECT p.cluster,
       COUNT(DISTINCT p.node_id) AS nodes_affected,
       COUNT(DISTINCT p.job_id) AS jobs_placed,
       COUNT(DISTINCT p.job_id) FILTER (WHERE j.final_state = 'failed') AS jobs_failed
FROM placed p
JOIN jobs j ON j.job_id = p.job_id
GROUP BY p.cluster
ORDER BY p.cluster;

NVD-L4-01.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Collection: a node agent samples per-GPU counters every {{sample_interval}} (correctable and uncorrectable memory errors, memory locations retired or remapped, interconnect link error counters, temperature, power) and tails the kernel log for driver error events. It sends them with node_id, gpu_serial, gpu_index, driver_version, boot_id, sample_ts. Including boot_id (or a driver-load id) lets the pipeline compute deltas that survive resets: a delta is value − previous within one boot, and value itself after a reset, never a negative number.
  • Normalisation: a versioned mapping from event code to class (hardware_fatal, hardware_degraded, application, unknown), owned by the platform team. Unknown codes are kept and counted, not dropped.
  • Job attribution: the scheduler's job events give, per job, the nodes and GPUs held and the exit reason. For a failed job, the attributor looks for (a) a hardware-class event on one of its GPUs within a window before the failure, (b) the first rank to stop heartbeating or to report an error, (c) link errors on a port the job's nodes share. Only (a), or (b) corroborated by repeated failures on the same node across different jobs, implicates a node. A timeout seen by every rank implicates no one by itself.
  • Detection rules: stateful rules over the normalised stream, each with an id and a version, for example: any hardware_fatal event → drain now; correctable-error rate above R per hour over a day (rate from deltas, not cumulative value) → drain at next job boundary; same node implicated in N distinct jobs' failures in a week → drain at next boundary. Rules run in shadow first; their would-be decisions are logged and compared with outcomes before they are allowed to act.
  • Action layer: a drain controller that enforces the {{drain_budget}} automatic budget, a rate limit (drains per 10 minutes), and a correlated-cause check: before draining, group candidates by shared switch, rack, power domain, driver version and recent change; if many candidates share one, stop and page a person with the grouping. Drain modes: immediate (fatal) or at the next checkpoint/job boundary (degraded), with a notice to the owners of running jobs. Beyond the budget, decisions queue for human approval.
  • Audit: every decision writes an immutable record: decision_id, node, gpus, rule_id, rule_version, the signal values and events that fired it (with their ids), automatic or approved by whom, jobs interrupted, time. Diagnostics outcome, repair actions and return-to-service are appended to the same node history.
  • Return to service: diagnostics pass → probation (placed only small or low-priority jobs, tighter thresholds) for 14 days; a recurrence during probation sends it to repair.
  • Measurement: label each drain later as confirmed bad (diagnostic failure, part replaced, or recurrence within probation) or not confirmed. Precision = confirmed / drained, by rule version. For false negatives, count hardware-confirmed faults found by other routes (repair tickets, diagnostics on scheduled maintenance, a fatal event after the rule should have fired) per node-month. Report both with the uncertainty from the diagnostic suite's own miss rate, estimated by re-testing a sample of passing nodes or by recurrence rates.

Competing designs to accept. A learned model (gradient-boosted trees or similar) over the same signals, if the candidate supplies labels, explanations per decision and the same action limits. Per-GPU drains for small jobs and per-node drains for large ones. A streaming engine versus a time-series database with periodic rule evaluation, if the five-minute fatal-event target holds.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Mass drains from a fleet-wide change; blaming every node in a failed job; counter resets hiding fast-growing errors; diagnostics that miss intermittent faults inflating apparent false positives; drains that kill large jobs right before a checkpoint; unknown event codes silently ignored.

Incident guidance.

  • Driver update makes a harmless code fire everywhere: the budget and the correlated-cause check should stop it after a few drains; group candidates by driver version and page the driver owners. Recover: mark the code as application or benign for that driver version in the mapping (a new mapping version), undrain nodes drained by it. Prevent: any mapping or rule change and any driver rollout runs in shadow first; alerts on drain proposals per hour.
  • Four drains, all healthy, one flapping link: attribution by "a node in the failed job" is wrong. Recover: undrain, look at link error counters on ports shared by the four jobs, take the port out. Prevent: require hardware evidence or repeat failures across different jobs for a node to be implicated; add link and switch-port counters to attribution; a rule that groups failures by shared fabric component.
  • Errors hidden by nightly resets: rules used cumulative values. Fix: deltas within a boot id; a rate rule over a rolling window; backfill the rate for the fleet to find other such GPUs, and quarantine the checkpoints written from that GPU's job (verify them).
  • 40% of drains pass diagnostics: it is a measurement problem first. Split by rule version and by signal: which rules have low confirmation? Use probation recurrence rates to estimate how many passes were intermittent faults. Adjust thresholds per rule with that evidence, and propose longer or stress-based diagnostics where intermittent faults dominate.
